title: Naso: lift up the heads (Numbers 4:22)
hookLine: the census phrase means both "count" and "lift up"

cards: In prison, in Genesis, Joseph listens to two men's dreams. To the royal cupbearer he says: in three days Pharaoh will lift up your head, and give you back your job.
To the royal baker he says: in three days Pharaoh will lift up your head, too. Then he finishes the sentence. Off you.
The same Hebrew phrase, lift up the head, means a pardon for one man and a hanging for the other. Hold on to that phrase. It comes back in this week's portion, and this time it's about counting.

teach.h: NASO ET ROSH: LIFT THE HEAD.
teach.b: The new portion is called Naso, from its first instruction. God tells Moses to take the sum of the sons of Gershon. In Hebrew: naso et rosh, literally, lift up the head.
It's a phrase the Torah uses for taking a census. You don't count heads; you lift them. The phrase has the double edge Joseph's dreams show.

Being counted can raise you up, or it can single you out. Some read the census itself as a choice about which it will be. To count someone well is to lift them: you matter, you're on the list, you belong.
Then look at who's being counted.
Gershon is named first among Levi's sons. Yet in the order of service, Kohath, the younger clan, was counted first, because Kohath carried the ark.
Gershon's clan carried the curtains, the coverings, the hangings and the ropes. Soft goods. Not glamorous.

And the verse adds two small Hebrew words: gam hem, them also. Take the sum of the sons of Gershon too. Some commentators read those words as a deliberate lift for the clan that might have felt second.
They count. Their load counts. The same root, nun, sin, alef, lift or carry, turns up again in these chapters as the word for bearing the sanctuary's loads.
It'll come back soon, in a blessing, when God lifts up a face. In Naso, to count is to carry, and to carry is to lift.

how: Naso is read in late spring, usually just after Shavuot. Its opening phrase, naso et rosh, is studied as a lesson in how being counted can lift a person up.

o: a curtain carried by the clan of Gershon
lift up: the Torah's way of saying count
the pardon given to Pharaoh's cupbearer

games.q: lifting the heads — tap the pairs.

s: the Hebrew for taking a census is lift up the head
naso et rosh: to count is, literally, to lift.
Kohath carried the ark; Gershon carried the curtains and coverings.
in Joseph's prison, lift up your head always meant good news
for the baker, it meant his head lifted off him.

games.q: Kohath, the younger clan, carries the ark and is counted first. Gershon, the eldest, carries curtains. how does the verse count Gershon?
o: it skips them; their work is minor.
it adds "them also": lift up their heads too.
it counts them with the other tribes.
games.why: naso et rosh bnei Gershon gam hem: lift up the heads of Gershon's sons too. some commentators hear a deliberate lift.

practice: Think of the people around you who carry the soft loads: the one who handles the paperwork, does the laundry, sends the reminders, keeps the group chat from falling apart. Pick one whose head could use lifting.
Find exactly what you'd say: not thanks for everything, but thanks for this, specifically.

wordCard.voice: Naso. Lift up: the word this week's portion is named for, the Bible's way of saying count, and its way of saying you matter.
